overview:
Vatican City is the smallest country in the world, covering about 0.44 km² and sitting entirely inside Rome, Italy. Its walls enclose St. Peter's Basilica, the wide oval of St. Peter's Square, the Vatican Museums, the Sistine Chapel and a large stretch of gardens. A person can walk from one side of the country to the other in roughly fifteen minutes.

Vatican City is the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church and the home of the pope, who leads the Church and is also head of state. Fewer than a thousand people live there, among them cardinals, priests, staff and the Swiss Guard, the soldiers in striped uniforms who protect the pope. Italian is used day to day, and Latin remains the official language of Church documents. Millions of visitors and pilgrims arrive each year, and for so small a place the Vatican keeps a great deal of its own: a post office, a newspaper, a radio station and a railway station.
landAndNature: There is almost no wild landscape in a country this small, but slightly more than half of the Vatican is garden. Behind the basilica lie about 23 hectares of lawns, clipped hedges, fountains, orange and olive trees, and stands of palm, oak and cedar planted over the centuries, along with a replica of the grotto at Lourdes. These gardens have been cultivated since the 1200s. Ring-necked parakeets, gulls and peregrine falcons nest on the rooftops and domes. The country sits on the Vatican Hill, a low rise on the west bank of the Tiber River, and has no rivers, coastline or farmland of its own.
peopleAndCulture: Life inside the Vatican follows the Church calendar. On many Sundays the pope appears at a window above St. Peter's Square to speak to the crowd below, and at Christmas and Easter the square fills with hundreds of thousands of people. The Sistine Chapel, painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512, is used for the conclave, the sealed meeting at which cardinals elect a new pope; black smoke from a chimney means no decision has been reached, white smoke means a pope has been chosen. The Vatican Museums hold one of the world's great art collections, and the Swiss Guard has protected popes since 1506.
history: Tradition holds that the apostle Peter was buried on this hill in Roman times, and a church was raised over the site in the 300s; the present St. Peter's Basilica was built between 1506 and 1626, with Michelangelo among its designers. For more than a thousand years popes governed the Papal States, a broad band of territory across central Italy. When Italy was unified in 1870 it absorbed those lands, and popes refused to leave the Vatican for nearly sixty years afterward. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 settled the dispute by recognizing Vatican City as an independent state. It has remained neutral in conflicts since and keeps diplomatic relations with most countries in the world.
funFacts: The whole of Vatican City would fit inside New York's Central Park nearly eight times over.
Vatican City has the shortest national railway in the world, a track about 300 meters long with one station.
The Swiss Guard, founded in 1506, is among the oldest military units still in continuous service anywhere.
Michelangelo spent four years painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling, working on scaffolding high above the floor.
Nobody is born a Vatican citizen; citizenship is granted for as long as a person works there and then ends.
The Vatican Library holds manuscripts more than a thousand years old on about 80 kilometers of shelving.
